title: Record-Shattering Spring Heat Wave Scorches Europe, Leaving Multiple Dead
summary: A spring heat wave of historic proportions is baking Western Europe, toppling temperature records that had stood for over a century. On Tuesday, the UK's Kew Gardens recorded a staggering 95.2°F (35.1°C), breaking the 94.6°F mark set just a day earlier—and shattering the previous May record of 91.4°F from 1922. London also experienced a rare "tropical night," with temperatures staying above 68°F. France saw the mercury hit 97°F, while Seville, Spain, reached 100°F over the weekend. Meteorologists say a "heat dome"—a high-pressure system that traps hot air—is responsible, pushing temperatures more than 10 degrees Celsius above normal. "We know beyond a shadow of a doubt that heat wave events such as this have been made more likely and more severe due to climate change," said Peter Thorne, director of the ICARUS Climate Research Centre at Maynooth University in Ireland. The unseasonable heat has turned deadly. In the UK, at least four teenagers drowned in lakes and reservoirs, and a 60-year-old man died in the sea. French officials reported at least seven heat-related deaths, including five drownings and two fatalities during sports competitions. The early timing means lifeguards are not yet on duty at many beaches, increasing the danger. The UK Health Security Agency issued an amber alert through Thursday, warning of health risks, especially for the elderly. Many British homes and businesses lack air conditioning, leaving people vulnerable. Commuters sweltered in London's un-air-conditioned subway cars, while firefighters battled a grass fire near Edinburgh's Arthur's Seat. As extreme weather becomes more frequent, experts say such events are a stark reminder of the urgent need to address climate change.
why_it_matters: Rising frequency of extreme heat directly threatens public health — especially for the elderly, outdoor workers, and those without air conditioning — and reveals how unprepared many cities are for a warming world, making adaptation and climate action critical for today's young people.

background_read: The 2003 European heat wave was one of the deadliest natural disasters on the continent in modern times, causing over 70,000 excess deaths, mostly among the elderly. Since then, heat waves have become more frequent and intense due to human-caused climate change.

Kew Gardens in London is a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the world's most famous botanical gardens; its weather station has reliable records stretching back over a century, making it a key site for measuring climate extremes.

The ICARUS Climate Research Centre at Maynooth University in Ireland specializes in studying how climate change affects extreme weather events, using data to show that many recent heat waves would be virtually impossible without global warming.

In the United Kingdom, air conditioning is rare in homes and even in parts of the London Underground (subway), because the country's climate was historically cool. As heat waves intensify, this lack of cooling infrastructure becomes a serious public health risk.

perspectives.description: Record-shattering heat provides undeniable evidence that may finally accelerate climate policies, push governments to invest in cooling centers, and encourage a faster shift toward renewable energy to reduce future warming.

The deaths and strain on hospitals show that preparedness is inadequate; many older buildings lack air conditioning, and the absence of early-season lifeguards exposes gaps in emergency planning that cost lives.

Heat domes themselves are natural weather patterns, but climate change raises background temperatures, making the same pattern produce far hotter conditions. The UK's housing stock and public transport were designed for a cooler climate, creating a systemic vulnerability.

Governments may need to mandate cooling in public housing, revise heat alert systems to activate earlier in the year, and redesign cities with more green spaces and reflective surfaces. For younger generations, this means both mitigating climate change and learning to live with its unavoidable consequences.
